interior-dirichlet-mode.title: Joint and marginal modes
interior-dirichlet-mode.prompt: For concentrations (2,3,5), what is the joint-mode first coordinate and what is the mode of P₁ alone?
interior-dirichlet-mode.answer: The joint-mode coordinate is 1/7. The marginal is Beta(2,8), whose mode is 1/8.

interior-dirichlet-mode.title: A uniform simplex density
interior-dirichlet-mode.prompt: Can the formula (αₖ−1)/(α₀−K) select a unique mode when every concentration equals one?
interior-dirichlet-mode.answer: No. It becomes 0/0. The density is constant, so the interior points all have the same density.

log-partition-moment-identities.title: A change of parameter
log-partition-moment-identities.prompt: Does differentiating A(log λ)=λ with respect to λ directly give the Poisson variance through the natural-parameter identity?
log-partition-moment-identities.answer: No. The identity uses derivatives with respect to η=log λ. Chain-rule factors are required when differentiating with respect to λ.

log-partition-moment-identities.title: A redundant statistic
log-partition-moment-identities.prompt: If T₂=2T₁ identically, can the covariance matrix of (T₁,T₂) be positive definite?
log-partition-moment-identities.answer: No. The nonzero direction (2,−1) has zero variance, so the covariance matrix is singular.

marginal-hyperposterior.title: A finite posterior weight
marginal-hyperposterior.prompt: Two candidate hyperparameter values have equal prior mass and likelihood kernels 1/18 and 3/50. What is the posterior probability of the second?

marginal-hyperposterior.title: Transforming a density
marginal-hyperposterior.prompt: Under α=mk and β=(1−m)k, what absolute Jacobian factor is required for a density in (m,k)?
marginal-hyperposterior.answer: The determinant has absolute value k, so multiply the (α,β) density evaluated at the inverse map by k.

marginal-student-posterior.title: Scale versus standard deviation
marginal-student-posterior.prompt: A Student posterior has three degrees of freedom and scale squared 5/6. What is its variance?

marginal-student-posterior.title: Residual degrees of freedom
marginal-student-posterior.prompt: In a full-rank Gaussian regression with n=12 responses and p=4 coefficients under the stated reference prior, what are the Student degrees of freedom?
marginal-student-posterior.answer: They are n−p=8, including the intercept among the four coefficients if the model has one.

normal-inverse-gamma-variance-update.title: Known mean and displaced observations
normal-inverse-gamma-variance-update.prompt: If observations are all close to 12 but the known mean is 10, can their near-zero sample variance replace Qμ in the update?
normal-inverse-gamma-variance-update.answer: No. Qμ includes the squared displacement of the sample mean from the known value. Centering at the sample mean would change the likelihood.

normal-inverse-gamma-variance-update.title: A proper law without a mean
normal-inverse-gamma-variance-update.prompt: Does an inverse-gamma posterior with shape 0.8 and positive scale have a finite posterior mean?
normal-inverse-gamma-variance-update.answer: No. It is a proper density, but its mean exists only when shape exceeds one.

normal-normal-conjugacy.title: A fractional equivalent sample
normal-normal-conjugacy.prompt: Observations have known variance 4 and the prior variance of the mean is 8. What equivalent prior sample size does that prior represent, and must the number be an integer?
normal-normal-conjugacy.answer: The equivalent count is the observation variance divided by the prior variance, 4/8=1/2. It need not be an integer: it counts prior precision in units of one observation, not rows secretly added to the data.

normal-normal-conjugacy.title: Observation order
normal-normal-conjugacy.prompt: Would processing 12 before 8 change the final posterior?
normal-normal-conjugacy.answer: No. Precision increments and precision-weighted-value increments add in either order.

posterior-prediction-under-the-reference.title: No new observation noise
posterior-prediction-under-the-reference.prompt: Why does an interval for the mean use h rather than 1+h?
posterior-prediction-under-the-reference.answer: The mean is a linear function of the coefficients. It has coefficient uncertainty but no new independent measurement error.

posterior-prediction-under-the-reference.title: A proper law without a variance
posterior-prediction-under-the-reference.prompt: For a Student predictive law with two degrees of freedom, can its scale be finite while its variance is infinite?
posterior-prediction-under-the-reference.answer: Yes. The distribution is proper, but a finite Student variance requires more than two degrees of freedom.

study-rate-full-conditional.title: Updating a second study
study-rate-full-conditional.prompt: Under Beta(2,3) hyperparameters, what is the full conditional after 2 successes in 8 trials?

study-rate-full-conditional.title: A larger prior sample size
study-rate-full-conditional.prompt: Keep the prior centre at 0.4 but set the concentration to 20. For 4 successes in 5 trials, what is the conditional mean?
study-rate-full-conditional.answer: The shapes are (8,12), so the mean is (4+8)/(5+20)=12/25=0.48.

a-finite-endpoint-and-a-weibull-extreme-.title: Which tail?
a-finite-endpoint-and-a-weibull-extreme-.prompt: For Y_n=n(1−M_n), does Y_n>2 mean the maximum is closer to or farther below the endpoint than 1−2/n?

a-finite-endpoint-and-a-weibull-extreme-.title: Changing the endpoint tail
a-finite-endpoint-and-a-weibull-extreme-.prompt: If 1−F(xF−t) is asymptotic to 3t², what is the natural gap scale a_n?
a-finite-endpoint-and-a-weibull-extreme-.answer: It is $(3n)^{-1/2}$, giving a limiting scaled-gap survival $e^{-y^2}$.

a-permutation-test.title: Monte Carlo spacing is not a standard error
a-permutation-test.prompt: A corrected Monte Carlo probability near 0.20 is computed from m=1999 random permutations. Using the binomial formula with proportion 0.20 and denominator 1999, what is the approximate standard error?
a-permutation-test.answer: About 0.00895, the square root of 0.2 times 0.8 over 1999. The grid spacing 1/2000 is a different quantity.

a-permutation-test.title: A mean null versus a symmetry null
a-permutation-test.prompt: Does equality of two population means by itself justify unrestricted label permutation?
a-permutation-test.answer: No. Exact permutation validity requires the specified distributional or randomisation invariance, which equality of means alone does not imply.

a-proper-approximation-to-the-flat-prior.title: Prior mass in a fixed interval
a-proper-approximation-to-the-flat-prior.prompt: For a uniform prior on [-20,20], what probability is assigned to [-3,3]?
a-proper-approximation-to-the-flat-prior.answer: The interval lengths are 6 and 40, so the probability is 3/20.

a-proper-approximation-to-the-flat-prior.title: Omitted likelihood mass
a-proper-approximation-to-the-flat-prior.prompt: A likelihood integrates to 5, of which 4 lies inside the prior window. What is the total-variation distance from the windowed posterior to the posterior that uses the whole likelihood?
a-proper-approximation-to-the-flat-prior.answer: The distance equals the omitted fraction 1 - 4/5 = 1/5.

acceptance-rejection-method.title: A tight envelope on a short interval
acceptance-rejection-method.prompt: The target density equals 4 on [0,1/4] and equals 0 elsewhere. The proposal is uniform on [0,1]. What is the smallest valid M, and what is the mean number of proposals per accepted draw?
acceptance-rejection-method.answer: The smallest M is 4, because the target height is 4 and the proposal density is 1. The mean number of proposals equals M, so it is 4.

acceptance-rejection-method.title: The cost of a loose envelope
acceptance-rejection-method.prompt: If the bound increases from 3/2 to 3 while the target and proposal stay the same, what happens to mean proposals per output?
acceptance-rejection-method.answer: It increases from 3/2 to 3, so the expected number doubles.

accidental-deaths-data.title: A supplied frequency
accidental-deaths-data.prompt: What does frequency 12 mean for the monthly USAccDeaths time series?
accidental-deaths-data.answer: It records twelve observations per year. It is time-series metadata, rather than a claim that an unindexed algorithm discovered the period.

accidental-deaths-data.title: A quadratic seasonal difference
accidental-deaths-data.prompt: For the series $Y_t=3t^2$, what is the ordinary difference of the lag-12 seasonal differences?
accidental-deaths-data.answer: The lag-12 difference is 72t - 432, and its ordinary difference is the constant 72.

adjusted-r-squared.title: Residual degrees of freedom
adjusted-r-squared.prompt: An intercept and five slopes are fitted to 40 observations. What are the residual degrees of freedom?
adjusted-r-squared.answer: Six coefficients are fitted, so the residual degrees of freedom are 40 - 6 = 34.

adjusted-r-squared.title: A negative adjusted score
adjusted-r-squared.prompt: With n=10, one slope, SST=9 and SSE=8.8, what is adjusted R-squared?
adjusted-r-squared.answer: It is 1-(8.8/8)/(9/9)=-0.1. A negative adjusted score is possible.

analysis-of-deviance.title: Another likelihood-ratio scale
analysis-of-deviance.prompt: If deviance decreases by 12 and the known dispersion is 3, what is the scaled likelihood-ratio statistic?

analysis-of-deviance.title: Rank difference
analysis-of-deviance.prompt: Two nested models have design ranks 5 and 8. What is the rank difference used for their regular likelihood-ratio comparison?
analysis-of-deviance.answer: It is 8-5=3, provided the models satisfy the regularity assumptions.

anova-sum-of-squares-decomposition.title: Three groups
anova-sum-of-squares-decomposition.prompt: Group means are 1, 4 and 10, with sizes 5, 1 and 4. What is the grand mean?

anova-sum-of-squares-decomposition.title: The zero cross-term
anova-sum-of-squares-decomposition.prompt: Why does the cross-term in the ANOVA decomposition vanish?
anova-sum-of-squares-decomposition.answer: Within each group, the deviations from that group mean sum to zero.

asymptotic-normality-of-maximum-likeliho.title: A derivative count
asymptotic-normality-of-maximum-likeliho.prompt: If $S_n=\ell_n\prime$, which log-likelihood derivative occurs in the quadratic Taylor remainder of the score?
asymptotic-normality-of-maximum-likeliho.answer: It is $S_n\prime\prime=\ell_n\prime\prime\prime$, the third log-likelihood derivative.

asymptotic-normality-of-maximum-likeliho.title: Why consistency is separate
asymptotic-normality-of-maximum-likeliho.prompt: Does solving the score equation prove that the resulting root converges to the true parameter?
asymptotic-normality-of-maximum-likeliho.answer: No. There may be several roots or local maxima. Consistency must identify the sequence to which the local expansion applies.

axioms-of-probability.title: The overlap correction
axioms-of-probability.prompt: Why must $P(A\cap B)$ be subtracted from $P(A)+P(B)$?
axioms-of-probability.answer: The intersection is counted once in each probability, but must be counted only once in the union.

axioms-of-probability.title: Uncountably many points
axioms-of-probability.prompt: Why can a uniform interval have total probability one although every singleton has probability zero?
axioms-of-probability.answer: Countable additivity governs countable disjoint unions. An interval is an uncountable union of singleton points, so that sum rule does not apply to the union over all its points.

batch-and-online-learning.title: A factor of sample size
batch-and-online-learning.prompt: For a sum loss, is the single uniformly drawn case gradient itself unbiased for the full gradient?
batch-and-online-learning.answer: No. Its expectation is the average gradient. Multiplying it by $n$ gives an unbiased estimate of the sum gradient.

batch-and-online-learning.title: A rising loss
batch-and-online-learning.prompt: Does one stochastic step that increases the full loss contradict gradient unbiasedness?
batch-and-online-learning.answer: No. Unbiasedness is an expectation over the sampled case at the fixed current weight; a particular sampled direction may increase the full loss.

bayes-consistency-of-nearest-neighbours.title: A local but noisy choice
bayes-consistency-of-nearest-neighbours.prompt: Does k_n=1 satisfy k_n→infinity and k_n/n→0?
bayes-consistency-of-nearest-neighbours.answer: Only the second condition holds. One neighbour does not average away label noise.

bayes-consistency-of-nearest-neighbours.title: An excess-error bound
bayes-consistency-of-nearest-neighbours.prompt: At a point where the true regression is 0.8 and the estimated regression is 0.4, the two classification rules disagree. What is the conditional excess error, and what upper bound does twice the absolute regression error give?
bayes-consistency-of-nearest-neighbours.answer: The conditional excess error is |1.6 - 1| = 0.6. Twice the absolute regression error is 2 times 0.4 = 0.8, which sits above 0.6.

bayes-factors-and-posterior-odds.title: An improper scale
bayes-factors-and-posterior-odds.prompt: Two models use improper priors that differ by a constant factor, and both parameter posteriors are proper. Does that factor cancel from the Bayes factor?
bayes-factors-and-posterior-odds.answer: No. An arbitrary prior scale multiplies the marginal likelihood. It cancels inside one model's parameter posterior when that posterior is proper, but it remains in a comparison between models.

bayes-factors-and-posterior-odds.title: Two kinds of priors
bayes-factors-and-posterior-odds.prompt: Which prior choice is absent from a Bayes factor but required to convert it into posterior model odds?
bayes-factors-and-posterior-odds.answer: Prior probabilities of the model labels. Within-model parameter priors remain part of the marginal likelihood and hence the Bayes factor.

benjamini-hochberg-controls-the-false-di.title: A realised proportion
benjamini-hochberg-controls-the-false-di.prompt: If R=20 hypotheses are rejected and V=3 are false rejections, what is the false-discovery proportion?
benjamini-hochberg-controls-the-false-di.answer: It is 3/20=0.15. This realised value is not the expectation defining FDR.

benjamini-hochberg-controls-the-false-di.title: No rejections
benjamini-hochberg-controls-the-false-di.prompt: Why is the false-discovery proportion set to zero when R=0?
benjamini-hochberg-controls-the-false-di.answer: There are no discoveries and no false discoveries. The definition uses V/(R∨1), which equals zero in that case.

birth-weight-data.title: A conditional comparison
birth-weight-data.prompt: What is held fixed when interpreting the smoking coefficient in this fitted model?
birth-weight-data.answer: Maternal weight, maternal age and the recorded race category. It compares fitted conditional means at equal values of those included predictors.

birth-weight-data.title: Age and a large probability
birth-weight-data.prompt: Does an age coefficient probability near $0.84$ prove that age has no relation to birth weight?
birth-weight-data.answer: No. It indicates weak evidence against a zero conditional linear coefficient in this specified model; it does not prove absence of an association in every model or population.

birthday-problem.title: One person or any pair?
birthday-problem.prompt: What is the probability that at least one of twenty-two people matches a specified host under the uniform 365-day model?
birthday-problem.answer: It is $1-(364/365)^{22}$; comparisons are all with the host, so this is a different event from any shared birthday.

birthday-problem.title: Probability versus pair count
birthday-problem.prompt: Can the expected number of matching pairs exceed one?
birthday-problem.answer: Yes. A single outcome can contain several matching pairs, so the pair count is not an indicator. Its expectation is $\binom n2/m$.

categorical-and-multinomial-models.title: A missing count
categorical-and-multinomial-models.prompt: Five observations are classified into four categories. Three of the counts are 2, 0 and 1. What is the remaining count?
categorical-and-multinomial-models.answer: The counts sum to the sample size, so the remaining count is 5 - 3 = 2.

categorical-and-multinomial-models.title: Predictive smoothing
categorical-and-multinomial-models.prompt: With a Dirichlet(1,1,1) prior and observed counts (4,0,0), what is the next-category probability for category two?
categorical-and-multinomial-models.answer: The posterior is Dirichlet(5,1,1), so that probability is 1/7.

chi-squared-test-for-a-variance.title: Power when the variance is halved
chi-squared-test-for-a-variance.prompt: A lower-tail 5% test of null variance 1.1 uses the chi-squared critical value on six degrees of freedom. If the true variance is half the null value, is the rejection probability above or below 5%?
chi-squared-test-for-a-variance.answer: Above 5%. At true variance 0.55 the power is about 0.226.

chi-squared-test-for-a-variance.title: Use the right units
chi-squared-test-for-a-variance.prompt: A specification states standard deviation 3. What variance belongs in the pivot denominator?
chi-squared-test-for-a-variance.answer: The variance is $3^2=9$. Dividing a squared sample standard deviation by 3 mixes units.

chi-squared-test-with-estimated-paramete.title: Which sample fits the parameter?
chi-squared-test-with-estimated-paramete.prompt: A test merges observations into five categories. From which likelihood should its parameter estimate be computed for the usual adjustment?
chi-squared-test-with-estimated-paramete.answer: The multinomial likelihood of those five category counts. An estimate from finer measurements need not give exactly the same reference law.

chi-squared-test-with-estimated-paramete.title: Saturated fit
chi-squared-test-with-estimated-paramete.prompt: With four categories and three independently fitted probability coordinates, how many residual degrees of freedom remain?
chi-squared-test-with-estimated-paramete.answer: There are $4-1-3=0$. The fitted vector can match all observed proportions, leaving no residual goodness-of-fit comparison.

chi-squared-test-with-known-cell-probabi.title: Count the constraints
chi-squared-test-with-known-cell-probabi.prompt: Why do four fixed positive cell probabilities give three chi-squared degrees of freedom?
chi-squared-test-with-known-cell-probabi.answer: The four count deviations sum to zero, leaving three free directions; no parameters are fitted from the counts.

chi-squared-test-with-known-cell-probabi.title: Zero expectation
chi-squared-test-with-known-cell-probabi.prompt: Can a category with null probability zero be inserted into the Pearson formula?
chi-squared-test-with-known-cell-probabi.answer: No. Its denominator is zero. A positive count there contradicts the null, and an impossible category with zero observed count can be removed before calculating the statistic.

choosing-the-number-of-principal-compone.title: A tie between leading eigenvalues
choosing-the-number-of-principal-compone.prompt: Eigenvalues are 4, 4, 1 and 1. What fraction of variance do the first two components explain, and does a rule requiring at least 90% stop at two?
choosing-the-number-of-principal-compone.answer: They explain 8/10=0.8. The rule needs the third component, which brings the total to 0.9.

choosing-the-number-of-principal-compone.title: Small variance and prediction
choosing-the-number-of-principal-compone.prompt: Can a discarded component with tiny predictor variance perfectly predict a response?
choosing-the-number-of-principal-compone.answer: Yes. The response can depend entirely on that direction. PCA orders predictor reconstruction variance without using the response.

classification-with-unequal-costs.title: Cost direction
classification-with-unequal-costs.prompt: What happens to the positive-class probability threshold when false negatives become more costly?
classification-with-unequal-costs.answer: It falls, because $C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})$ decreases as $C_{FN}$ increases.

classification-with-unequal-costs.title: Matrix orientation
classification-with-unequal-costs.prompt: Why must a loss matrix state which axis indexes truth?
classification-with-unequal-costs.answer: Reversing true and predicted indices exchanges the two error costs and can reverse the decision threshold.

conditional-distribution-of-a-multivaria.title: The conditioning value
conditional-distribution-of-a-multivaria.prompt: With mean blocks 1 and 2, cross-covariance 3 and conditioning variance 9, what is the conditional mean when X_B=8?

conditional-distribution-of-a-multivaria.title: A correlation calculation
conditional-distribution-of-a-multivaria.prompt: The variable being predicted has marginal variance 16, and its correlation with the conditioning variable is 1/2. What is its conditional variance?

conjugacy-is-optional.title: Normalising a posterior
conjugacy-is-optional.prompt: If the unnormalised posterior kernel integrates to 7/15, what factor turns it into a density?

conjugacy-is-optional.title: A beta update
conjugacy-is-optional.prompt: A Beta(1,1) prior is updated by two successes and one failure. What is the posterior, and what is its mean?
conjugacy-is-optional.answer: The posterior is Beta(3,2), and its mean is 3/5.

contingency-tables.title: Margins under independence
contingency-tables.prompt: Why must the fitted expected row totals equal the observed row totals?
contingency-tables.answer: Because $\sum_jR_iC_j/n=R_i\sum_jC_j/n=R_i$. The model fits each marginal distribution.

contingency-tables.title: Sampling unit
contingency-tables.prompt: Why is a table of repeated visits by the same patients unsuitable for an ordinary multinomial test without further assumptions?
contingency-tables.answer: Visits from the same patient can be dependent. The ordinary test treats the classified units as independent draws.

coverage.title: One interval
coverage.prompt: Does an observed 95% interval contain the parameter with a frequentist probability of 0.95?
coverage.answer: The parameter and observed endpoints are fixed. The 0.95 describes the random procedure over repeated samples under its assumptions.

coverage.title: Monte Carlo uncertainty
coverage.prompt: If a correctly calibrated rule misses in 7 of 100 independent runs, does that alone refute nominal 95% coverage?
coverage.answer: No. The number covering is random. It has a binomial distribution under independent repetitions; assess the deviation relative to that sampling variation.

d-p-q-and-r-functions.title: Shape, rate and scale
d-p-q-and-r-functions.prompt: A gamma law has shape 3 and rate 2. What is its mean, and what scale describes the same law?
d-p-q-and-r-functions.answer: The mean is 3/2. The equivalent scale is 1/2.

d-p-q-and-r-functions.title: Density units
d-p-q-and-r-functions.prompt: Why is dnorm(0) not the probability of drawing exactly zero?
d-p-q-and-r-functions.answer: It is a density height. A normal distribution gives a single point probability zero; an interval probability is an integral or a difference of CDF values.

delta-method.title: The derivative enters squared
delta-method.prompt: A root-n estimate has limiting variance 4. For h(t)=3t−2, what is the transformed limiting variance?

delta-method.title: A zero derivative
delta-method.prompt: For $h(\mu)=\mu^2$ at $\mu=0$ in a normal sample with variance $\sigma^2$, what is the law of $n$ times the squared sample mean divided by $\sigma^2$?
delta-method.answer: It is exactly chi-squared with one degree of freedom.

descent-of-lloyd-s-algorithm.title: Three assigned points
descent-of-lloyd-s-algorithm.prompt: What centre minimises the sum of squared distances for the values 1, 1 and 4, and what is that minimised sum?
descent-of-lloyd-s-algorithm.answer: The centre is their mean, 2. The minimised sum is 6.

descent-of-lloyd-s-algorithm.title: Objective convergence
descent-of-lloyd-s-algorithm.prompt: Does a decreasing objective bounded below by zero establish that Lloyd's algorithm finds the global optimum?
descent-of-lloyd-s-algorithm.answer: No. It establishes convergence of objective values; different starts can reach different stationary configurations.

detailed-balance-implies-stationarity.title: From balance to stationarity
detailed-balance-implies-stationarity.prompt: Detailed balance says π_i P_ij = π_j P_ji for every pair of states. Why does summing over i show that π is stationary?
detailed-balance-implies-stationarity.answer: The left-hand side becomes the j-th entry of πP. The right-hand side is π_j times a row sum of one, so πP = π.

detailed-balance-implies-stationarity.title: The converse
detailed-balance-implies-stationarity.prompt: Does every stationary Markov chain satisfy detailed balance?
detailed-balance-implies-stationarity.answer: No. A uniform stationary distribution for a directed three-state cycle has unequal opposite-edge flows.

draws-from-the-usual-families.title: Rate and scale
draws-from-the-usual-families.prompt: For a fixed $U$, what happens to $-\log(U)/\lambda$ when $\lambda$ doubles?
draws-from-the-usual-families.answer: The generated waiting time halves, consistent with $\lambda$ being a rate.

draws-from-the-usual-families.title: Another discrete inversion
draws-from-the-usual-families.prompt: Masses (0.1, 0.2, 0.7) sit at outcomes (0, 1, 2). What does U=0.25 produce?
draws-from-the-usual-families.answer: The cumulative thresholds are 0.1, 0.3 and 1. Since 0.25 lies between 0.1 and 0.3, the outcome is 1.

drift-and-scale-of-a-random-walk.title: Scale versus precision
drift-and-scale-of-a-random-walk.prompt: Does the spread of the position decrease as the number of steps grows?
drift-and-scale-of-a-random-walk.answer: No. Its standard deviation grows as $\sqrt n$. The average increment becomes more precise because dividing the position change by $n$ reduces its standard deviation to $\sigma/\sqrt n$.

drift-and-scale-of-a-random-walk.title: Four hundred steps
drift-and-scale-of-a-random-walk.prompt: Step mean 0.2 and step variance 0.96. After 400 steps, what are the mean position change and the standard deviation of the position?
drift-and-scale-of-a-random-walk.answer: The mean change is 80. The standard deviation is the square root of 384, about 19.596.

error-and-residual.title: An observed gap
error-and-residual.prompt: If a response is 12 and its fitted conditional mean is 9, what is the residual? Can the true error be read off from those two values?
error-and-residual.answer: The residual is 3. The true error also needs the unknown true conditional mean, so it cannot generally be recovered.

error-and-residual.title: A different leverage
error-and-residual.prompt: An error variance is 4 and one diagonal leverage is 1/4. What is the variance of that residual?

expectation-of-a-function.title: Why the mean is not enough
expectation-of-a-function.prompt: If g is not a linear function, why can the average of g(X) not be recovered from the average of X alone?
expectation-of-a-function.answer: Different distributions can share a mean and still give different averages of g. The average of g uses the distribution of X.

expectation-of-a-function.title: A two-point square
expectation-of-a-function.prompt: X equals 0 or 6 with probabilities 1/3 and 2/3. What are $E(X)$, $E(X^2)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$?
expectation-of-a-function.answer: The mean is 4, the second moment is 24, and the variance is 8.

exploratory-data-analysis.title: Sensitivity to an extreme value
exploratory-data-analysis.prompt: For 2,3,3,4,50, which of the mean and median changes when 50 becomes 500?
exploratory-data-analysis.answer: The mean increases from 12.4 to 102.4. The median remains 3.

exploratory-data-analysis.title: A clue and a conclusion
exploratory-data-analysis.prompt: A scatterplot suggests a curved association. Does that observation alone establish a causal effect?
exploratory-data-analysis.answer: No. It suggests a relationship to investigate; causality also needs assumptions and evidence about treatment assignment, confounding and the data-generating process.

extended-information-criterion.title: Which likelihood
extended-information-criterion.prompt: Why should the graphical-lasso penalised objective not be substituted for the maximised likelihood in EBIC?
extended-information-criterion.answer: It includes shrinkage and a fitting penalty. The stated EBIC compares unpenalised constrained maximum-likelihood fits on the candidate edge sets.

extended-information-criterion.title: What the extra charge counts
extended-information-criterion.prompt: If $p$ increases while $n$ and the fitted edge count stay fixed, what happens to EBIC when $\gamma>0$?
extended-information-criterion.answer: The extra term $4\gamma|E|\log p$ increases, reflecting the larger space of possible graph edges.

fallacy-of-the-transposed-conditional.title: Equal conditionals
fallacy-of-the-transposed-conditional.prompt: If $P(A\cap B)=0.1$, $P(A)=0.2$ and $P(B)=0.5$, calculate $P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B\mid A)$.

fallacy-of-the-transposed-conditional.title: A rare condition
fallacy-of-the-transposed-conditional.prompt: With sensitivity 0.9 and false-positive probability 0.05 fixed, does lowering prevalence increase or decrease positive predictive value?
fallacy-of-the-transposed-conditional.answer: It decreases positive predictive value, because false positives account for a larger fraction of positive results.

fixed-rule-error.title: Reweight without refitting
fixed-rule-error.prompt: A fixed rule has class-conditional error rates 0.05 and 0.50. What is its overall error if the future prevalences are 0.9 and 0.1, and what is it if the two classes are equally common?
fixed-rule-error.answer: The prevalence-weighted error is 0.9×0.05+0.1×0.50=0.095. Equal weights give (0.05+0.50)/2=0.275. The conditional rates did not change.

fixed-rule-error.title: Conditional and algorithmic error
fixed-rule-error.prompt: If the training data are sampled again and the rule is refitted, is that the same target as the error of one fixed fitted rule?
fixed-rule-error.answer: No. It averages over a distribution of fitted rules rather than conditioning on one realised rule.

forward-equations-of-the-poisson-process.title: Where is the inflow?
forward-equations-of-the-poisson-process.prompt: Why does the equation for count n contain p_(n-1), rather than p_(n+1)?
forward-equations-of-the-poisson-process.answer: Only upward unit jumps are possible. Probability enters n from n-1 and leaves n for n+1.

forward-equations-of-the-poisson-process.title: Empty interval
forward-equations-of-the-poisson-process.prompt: For a homogeneous Poisson process of rate λ, which count probability equals the probability that the first arrival is after time t?
forward-equations-of-the-poisson-process.answer: The probability of zero arrivals, $e^{-\lambda t}$. The first arrival is later than t exactly when the count at t is zero.

four-state-random-walk.title: Matrix convention
four-state-random-walk.prompt: For the displayed column-stochastic matrix, how is a probability column advanced?
four-state-random-walk.answer: Multiply on the left by $Q$: $v_{t+1}=Qv_t$. Stationarity is $Q\pi=\pi$.

four-state-random-walk.title: Uniform equilibrium?
four-state-random-walk.prompt: Why does the uniform distribution fail for this walk?
four-state-random-walk.answer: Endpoints have one neighbor and interior states have two. Pairwise flow balance requires each interior state to carry twice an endpoint's probability.

four-ways-of-counting-draws.title: A repeated label
four-ways-of-counting-draws.prompt: Does a set {A,A,B} distinguish two copies of A from one?
four-ways-of-counting-draws.answer: No. Sets remove repeated membership; the outcome must be represented by a multiset or a count vector.

four-ways-of-counting-draws.title: Order without replacement
four-ways-of-counting-draws.prompt: How many ordered triples of distinct labels can be drawn from five labels?

fubini-s-theorem.title: A tail that never integrates
fubini-s-theorem.prompt: A nonnegative lifetime has survival function $1/(1+t)$ for $t\ge0$. Is its expected lifetime finite?
fubini-s-theorem.answer: No. The integral from zero to $b$ is $\log(1+b)$, which diverges as $b$ increases. Tonelli still gives the identity with value infinity.

fubini-s-theorem.title: The other triangle
fubini-s-theorem.prompt: A joint density equals 2 on 0<y<x<1 and equals 0 elsewhere. If x is integrated first, what are the limits, and what is the integral?
fubini-s-theorem.answer: For each y between 0 and 1, x runs from y to 1. The integral of 2 over that region is 1.

gambler-s-ruin.title: A fair game from four
gambler-s-ruin.prompt: In a fair unit-step game stopped at zero or ten, starting at four, find the probability of reaching ten and the expected number of plays.
gambler-s-ruin.answer: The success probability is $4/10=0.4$ and the expected duration is $4(10-4)=24$ plays.

gambler-s-ruin.title: The boundary case
gambler-s-ruin.prompt: A gambler starts at the upper target $d$. What are the stopping time and success probability?
gambler-s-ruin.answer: The stopping time is zero and the success probability is one. No further play is needed.

general-linear-hypothesis.title: Redundant constraints
general-linear-hypothesis.prompt: Does repeating the same linear constraint double the numerator degrees of freedom?
general-linear-hypothesis.answer: No. The rank of the restriction matrix counts independent restrictions; duplicate rows add no dimension.

general-linear-hypothesis.title: F and the matching t
general-linear-hypothesis.prompt: A single linear restriction produces F=9 on (1, 20) degrees of freedom, using the same residual variance as the t statistic. What is the absolute t statistic?
general-linear-hypothesis.answer: 3, because that F statistic is the square of the t statistic.

generated-and-borel-sigma-algebras.title: Five atoms
generated-and-borel-sigma-algebras.prompt: A finite partition has five nonempty atoms. How many events are in the sigma-algebra it generates?
generated-and-borel-sigma-algebras.answer: Each atom can be included or excluded, so there are $2^5=32$ events.

generated-and-borel-sigma-algebras.title: Recover a point from half-lines
generated-and-borel-sigma-algebras.prompt: How can $\{a\}$ be obtained from half-lines of the form $(-\infty,b]$ using countable operations?
generated-and-borel-sigma-algebras.answer: Write $(-\infty,a)=\bigcup_{n\ge1}(-\infty,a-1/n]$ and subtract that set from $(-\infty,a]$. The difference is $\{a\}$.

hard-margin-primal.title: An irrelevant distant point
hard-margin-primal.prompt: For negative x=-2 and positive x=4, add another positive point at x=7. Does w=1/3, b=-1/3 remain feasible and optimal?
hard-margin-primal.answer: Yes. Its signed score is 2 at x=7, so the new constraint is slack. The two closer points still force w≥1/3.

hard-margin-primal.title: Contradictory labels
hard-margin-primal.prompt: What happens if an observation at x=4 is also assigned the negative label?
hard-margin-primal.answer: The score at 4 would have to satisfy f(4)≥1 and f(4)≤−1 simultaneously. The hard-margin constraints are infeasible.

hartigan-wong-algorithm.title: A singleton cannot donate
hartigan-wong-algorithm.prompt: Why must a transfer avoid removing the only point in its source cluster?
hartigan-wong-algorithm.answer: Removing it would create an empty cluster and violate the fixed number of nonempty clusters. The removal formula also has denominator zero at source size one.

hartigan-wong-algorithm.title: Apply both size factors
hartigan-wong-algorithm.prompt: A point has squared distance nine from a source centre of size three, and squared distance sixteen from a destination centre of size two. Is the transfer an improvement?
hartigan-wong-algorithm.answer: The saving is $(3/2)9=13.5$, while the cost is $(2/3)16=32/3$. The total change is $32/3-27/2=-17/6<0$, so it improves the objective.

heart-failure-data.title: Follow-up time
heart-failure-data.prompt: Why can a completed follow-up duration be unsuitable for a prediction made at admission?
heart-failure-data.answer: It may contain information that becomes available only after admission and can depend on when the outcome occurs. The prediction time and target horizon must be defined first.

heart-failure-data.title: One year from a low baseline
heart-failure-data.prompt: The fitted annual age odds multiplier is 1.0473. Starting from probability 0.10, what is the probability after that multiplier, to four decimals?

high-dimensional-data.title: Rank after centring
high-dimensional-data.prompt: For n=5 observations and p=12 features, what covariance rank is possible?
high-dimensional-data.answer: The rank is at most min(4,12)=4, so at least eight eigenvalues are zero.

high-dimensional-data.title: What ridge changes
high-dimensional-data.prompt: If covariance eigenvalues are (3,1,0), what are they after adding 0.2 times the identity?
high-dimensional-data.answer: They become (3.2,1.2,0.2), so the regularised matrix is positive definite.

homogeneity-and-independence.title: Three clinics
homogeneity-and-independence.prompt: Forty subjects are recruited from each of three clinics and classified into two outcomes. Which null matches the design, and how many degrees of freedom does the usual Pearson comparison have?
homogeneity-and-independence.answer: The null is homogeneity of the three outcome distributions, because each clinic sample size was fixed. The degrees of freedom are (3-1)(2-1)=2.

homogeneity-and-independence.title: Why the fitted counts agree
homogeneity-and-independence.prompt: Under independence in one multinomial sample, why do the fitted counts still equal row total times column total divided by the grand total?
homogeneity-and-independence.answer: The maximum-likelihood cell probabilities factor into a row proportion times a column proportion. Multiplying by the sample size produces that product of margins.

independent-events.title: Probability-zero event
independent-events.prompt: An event A has probability zero and B has probability 0.7. What is P(A∩B), and are they independent?
independent-events.answer: Monotonicity gives P(A∩B)=0=P(A)P(B). They are independent, without requiring an elementary conditional probability given A.

independent-events.title: Exclusive positive events
independent-events.prompt: Two disjoint events have probabilities 0.2 and 0.3. Can they be independent?
independent-events.answer: No. Their intersection probability is zero, while the product is 0.06.

ingredients-of-a-hypothesis-test.title: Model versus null
ingredients-of-a-hypothesis-test.prompt: Why should a model for a normal mean leave the mean unknown rather than set it equal to the tested value immediately?
ingredients-of-a-hypothesis-test.answer: The model must represent possible null and alternative parameter values. The null restriction is imposed when deriving the reference distribution.

ingredients-of-a-hypothesis-test.title: Power is a different probability
ingredients-of-a-hypothesis-test.prompt: Rejection is still X at least 13 in 15 serves. If the true success probability is 0.8, what is the approximate probability of rejection?
ingredients-of-a-hypothesis-test.answer: About 0.398. That is power at 0.8, not the null tail probability.

interval-for-a-difference-of-means.title: Why pool?
interval-for-a-difference-of-means.prompt: What assumption allows the two residual sums of squares to estimate the same parameter?
interval-for-a-difference-of-means.answer: Both populations have the same variance. Without it, the pooled variance is not estimating a common population variance.

interval-for-a-difference-of-means.title: Pairing
interval-for-a-difference-of-means.prompt: Two samples have the same number of observations. Must their analysis use paired differences?
interval-for-a-difference-of-means.answer: No. Pairing requires a meaningful match of observational units supplied by the design. Matching sample sizes alone is insufficient.

interval-for-a-normal-variance.title: Endpoint order
interval-for-a-normal-variance.prompt: Which chi-squared quantile belongs in the lower endpoint for the variance?
interval-for-a-normal-variance.answer: The upper quantile, because the variance appears in the denominator of the pivot.

interval-for-a-normal-variance.title: Change of scale
interval-for-a-normal-variance.prompt: Does taking square roots of the variance endpoints preserve coverage for standard deviation?
interval-for-a-normal-variance.answer: Yes. Square root is increasing on positive values, so both intervals describe the same inclusion event.

interval-for-a-proportion.title: Score interval at eight successes
interval-for-a-proportion.prompt: For 8 successes in 10 trials and $z=1.96$, where does the Wald interval go, and where does the Wilson interval sit?
interval-for-a-proportion.answer: The plug-in standard error is $0.126491$. The Wald interval is about $(0.5521,1.0479)$ before clipping, so the upper end leaves the unit interval. The Wilson interval is about $(0.4902,0.9433)$, inside $(0,1)$.

interval-for-a-proportion.title: Two groups
interval-for-a-proportion.prompt: Why are the estimated variances added in a two-proportion interval?
interval-for-a-proportion.answer: The difference of independent estimates has variance equal to the sum of their variances. Dependence would introduce a covariance term.

interval-for-a-ratio-of-variances.title: Swap populations
interval-for-a-ratio-of-variances.prompt: What changes when populations 1 and 2 are interchanged?
interval-for-a-ratio-of-variances.answer: The estimated and target ratios are reciprocated, the endpoint order reverses, and the numerator and denominator degrees of freedom swap.

interval-for-a-ratio-of-variances.title: Equality in a wide interval
interval-for-a-ratio-of-variances.prompt: An interval includes 1 and 10. Does it establish equal variances?
interval-for-a-ratio-of-variances.answer: No. Equality is compatible with the data, but so are large departures from equality. The interval indicates weak precision.

jackknife-bias-and-standard-error.title: Pseudovalues of a mean
jackknife-bias-and-standard-error.prompt: For the sample mean of observations 1,2,6, what are the three jackknife pseudovalues?
jackknife-bias-and-standard-error.answer: They are 1,2,6 themselves, because n x̄−(n−1)x̄₍₋ᵢ₎=xᵢ.

jackknife-bias-and-standard-error.title: Direction of correction
jackknife-bias-and-standard-error.prompt: If a full-sample statistic is 9 and its estimated jackknife bias is 7/3, what is the bias-corrected value?

joint-distribution-and-density.title: Probability from four corners
joint-distribution-and-density.prompt: Express $\Pr(a<X\le b,c<Y\le d)$ using the joint CDF.
joint-distribution-and-density.answer: It is $F(b,d)-F(a,d)-F(b,c)+F(a,c)$. The final term restores the overlap subtracted twice.

joint-distribution-and-density.title: Smooth margins on a diagonal
joint-distribution-and-density.prompt: If $X$ is uniform on $(0,1)$ and $Y=X$, does $(X,Y)$ have a two-dimensional Lebesgue density?
joint-distribution-and-density.answer: No. The pair assigns probability one to a diagonal of area zero, although both marginal laws have densities.

k-means-as-a-limiting-case.title: Unequal tie weights
k-means-as-a-limiting-case.prompt: With fixed weights $0.9$ and $0.1$, what limiting memberships does an observation exactly equidistant from the two centres receive as the common variance shrinks?
k-means-as-a-limiting-case.answer: The memberships stay in proportion to the weights, $0.9$ and $0.1$. A unique nearer centre still tends to membership one. The equal-weight limit of one half is the special case of equal weights.

k-means-as-a-limiting-case.title: Which update minimizes?
k-means-as-a-limiting-case.prompt: Why does the arithmetic mean appear in the hard M step?
k-means-as-a-limiting-case.answer: For a fixed cluster, squared-error loss equals its value at the sample mean plus the cluster size times the squared distance from that mean. The added term is minimized at zero.

k-means-criterion.title: One centre per observation
k-means-criterion.prompt: What is the within-cluster cost if every observation forms its own cluster?
k-means-criterion.answer: It is zero. Every point equals its own cluster mean, so all squared distances vanish.

k-means-criterion.title: Equal training cost
k-means-criterion.prompt: Two partitions have the same within-cluster sum of squares. What further comparison is needed before treating them as equally useful descriptions?
k-means-criterion.answer: Compare how many clusters each uses, or apply a penalty for extra clusters. Equal training scatter does not by itself prefer the simpler partition.

kernel-density-discriminant-analysis.title: Unequal sampling fractions
kernel-density-discriminant-analysis.prompt: Why does $n_g/n$ cancel $1/n_g$ with empirical priors and common bandwidth?
kernel-density-discriminant-analysis.answer: The class score is $(n_g/n)(1/n_g)\sum K_H=n^{-1}\sum K_H$. A deployment prior different from the training fraction does not give that cancellation.

kernel-density-discriminant-analysis.title: Posterior threshold
kernel-density-discriminant-analysis.prompt: If the density ratio $\widehat f_2/\widehat f_1$ is $4$ and the priors are $0.8,0.2$, what is the decision?
kernel-density-discriminant-analysis.answer: The scores are equal: $0.8\widehat f_1=0.2(4\widehat f_1)$. Both posterior probabilities are $1/2$, so zero–one loss leaves a tie.

kernel-support-vector-machine.title: Valid kernel check
kernel-support-vector-machine.prompt: Why must every finite Gram matrix of an inner-product kernel be positive semidefinite?

kernel-support-vector-machine.title: Free support vector
kernel-support-vector-machine.prompt: Which training point permits $b=y_k-\sum_i\alpha_i y_iK(x_i,x_k)$ in a soft-margin fit?
kernel-support-vector-machine.answer: Any point with $0<\alpha_k<C$. Its slack is zero and its margin constraint is an equality. A point at the upper bound need not satisfy the same equality.

large-sample-intervals.title: Coverage event
large-sample-intervals.prompt: Why can the interval include or miss the same fixed $\mu$ in repeated samples?
large-sample-intervals.answer: The sample mean and sample standard deviation vary across samples, so the endpoints vary. The population mean stays fixed.

large-sample-intervals.title: Sampling dependence
large-sample-intervals.prompt: If observations arrive in highly correlated household clusters, does increasing $n$ justify using $s/\sqrt n$?
large-sample-intervals.answer: No. The variance of the mean includes within-cluster covariance. A design-appropriate standard error or an explicit dependence model is required.

leaf-blotch-data.title: Degrees of freedom
leaf-blotch-data.prompt: How many residual degrees of freedom does the additive 10-variety, 9-site model have with one observation in each cell?
leaf-blotch-data.answer: There are 90 observations and 1+9+8=18 main-effect coefficients, so 72 residual degrees of freedom.

leaf-blotch-data.title: Constant scoring weight
leaf-blotch-data.prompt: Why does V(μ)=μ²(1−μ)² give a constant scoring weight with the logit link?
leaf-blotch-data.answer: The logit inverse has derivative μ(1−μ). Squaring that derivative gives V(μ), so their ratio equals one.

least-squares-decomposition.title: Change along a null direction
least-squares-decomposition.prompt: If $Xd=0$, how much does SSE change on replacing a fitted coefficient by $\widehat\beta+d$?
least-squares-decomposition.answer: It does not change, because the added term is $\|Xd\|^2=0$. Coefficient uniqueness therefore requires full column rank.

least-squares-decomposition.title: A known extra length
least-squares-decomposition.prompt: The least-squares residual has squared length 4. A competing coefficient differs by a vector d with squared fitted length 9, and the residual is orthogonal to the columns of the design. What is the competing residual sum of squares?
least-squares-decomposition.answer: It is 4+9=13. Orthogonality removes the cross term.

least-squares-estimators-are-unbiased.title: Changing only the error variances
least-squares-estimators-are-unbiased.prompt: Three independent errors have mean zero and variances 1, 4 and 9. Are the ordinary least-squares coefficient estimators unbiased?
least-squares-estimators-are-unbiased.answer: Yes. Unbiasedness uses their zero means and full rank. Their covariance becomes A diag(1,4,9) Aᵀ rather than AAᵀ.

least-squares-estimators-are-unbiased.title: Does one fit reveal bias?
least-squares-estimators-are-unbiased.prompt: One observed slope is 2.8 when the model slope is 2. Does this observation alone show that the estimator is biased?
least-squares-estimators-are-unbiased.answer: No. Bias compares the expectation across repeated samples with the model coefficient. Individual unbiased estimates can differ substantially from the coefficient.

lebesgue-decomposition.title: A density with missing mass
lebesgue-decomposition.prompt: A law has an atom of mass $0.3$ at zero and a density integrating to $0.7$. What mass remains for a singular continuous component?
lebesgue-decomposition.answer: Zero, because the total probability is one and $0.3+0.7=1$.

lebesgue-decomposition.title: A continuous CDF without a density
lebesgue-decomposition.prompt: Does a continuous CDF with derivative zero almost everywhere necessarily describe a point mass?
lebesgue-decomposition.answer: No. The Cantor law has a continuous CDF and no atoms, yet is supported on a Lebesgue-null set and has derivative zero almost everywhere.

levy-s-continuity-theorem.title: A point-mass transform
levy-s-continuity-theorem.prompt: The characteristic functions of $Y_n$ converge to $e^{3it}$ for every real $t$. What is the limiting law?
levy-s-continuity-theorem.answer: The limit is continuous at zero and is the characteristic function of the constant 3. Thus $Y_n$ converges in distribution to a point mass at 3.

levy-s-continuity-theorem.title: The missing continuity
levy-s-continuity-theorem.prompt: For $X_n\sim N(0,n)$, what happens to the characteristic function at $t=0$ and at a fixed $t\ne 0$?
levy-s-continuity-theorem.answer: It stays one at zero and tends to zero elsewhere. The discontinuity at zero prevents applying the converse continuity theorem.

lidar-data.title: Different bandwidths for different targets
lidar-data.prompt: Why can estimating pollutant concentration require a different smoothing bandwidth from estimating the mean log ratio?
lidar-data.answer: Concentration is related to a derivative of the mean curve. A derivative estimator has different weights and noise amplification, so its bias–variance balance can favour a different bandwidth.

lidar-data.title: Inclusive endpoints
lidar-data.prompt: An inclusive window of half-width 10 metres is centred at a recorded range of 200 metres. Which ranges does the window contain?
lidar-data.answer: It contains ranges from 190 metres through 210 metres, including both endpoints. How many observations that selects depends on the recorded ranges.

limits-of-sequences-of-events.title: Complement duality
limits-of-sequences-of-events.prompt: What is the complement of the event that $A_n$ occurs infinitely often?
limits-of-sequences-of-events.answer: It is $\liminf A_n^c$, the event that from some index onward none of the $A_n$ occurs.

limits-of-sequences-of-events.title: Equal probabilities without a set limit
limits-of-sequences-of-events.prompt: On a fair two-outcome space, alternate $\{H\}$ and $\{T\}$. What are the probability and set limits?
limits-of-sequences-of-events.answer: Every event has probability $1/2$, but the liminf is empty and the limsup is the whole space. There is no set limit.

linear-images-of-a-normal-vector.title: A zero contrast variance
linear-images-of-a-normal-vector.prompt: If a jointly normal vector has $a^\top\Sigma a=0$, what is the distribution of $a^\top X$?
linear-images-of-a-normal-vector.answer: It equals $a^\top\mu$ almost surely. This is a degenerate normal distribution with zero variance.

linear-images-of-a-normal-vector.title: Coefficient uncertainty in prediction
linear-images-of-a-normal-vector.prompt: If $Y=\beta+\varepsilon$, with independent $\beta\sim N(2,3)$ and $\varepsilon\sim N(0,4)$, what is the distribution of $Y$?
linear-images-of-a-normal-vector.answer: The sum is normal with mean two and variance $3+4=7$, so $Y\sim N(2,7)$.

linear-separability.title: Rescaling a separator
linear-separability.prompt: For $w=(3,4)$ and minimum functional margin $2$, what is the geometric margin?
linear-separability.answer: The norm is $5$, so the margin is $2/5=0.4$. Positive rescaling of both weights and bias leaves it unchanged.

linear-separability.title: Coincident observations
linear-separability.prompt: Can identical input vectors with opposite labels be strictly separated?
linear-separability.answer: No. The same affine score would need to be both positive and negative.

local-minima-plateaus-and-symmetry.title: Zero curvature
local-minima-plateaus-and-symmetry.prompt: For $L(t)=t^4$, what are the gradient and second derivative at zero, and is zero a minimum?
local-minima-plateaus-and-symmetry.answer: Both derivatives are zero, yet $t^4\ge 0$ with equality only at zero. Zero is a strict global minimum; the Hessian test is inconclusive.

local-minima-plateaus-and-symmetry.title: When two units stay equal
local-minima-plateaus-and-symmetry.prompt: Two hidden units have identical incoming and outgoing parameters. Do common minibatches alone make a deterministic gradient optimizer distinguish them?
local-minima-plateaus-and-symmetry.answer: No. Each minibatch produces the same paired derivatives, so identical updates preserve the equality. A source of asymmetry is required.

logistic-lasso.title: Zero-coordinate condition
logistic-lasso.prompt: A zero coefficient has smooth-loss gradient $0.03$ with $\lambda=0.05$. Does its coordinate violate the lasso optimality condition?
logistic-lasso.answer: No. The gradient magnitude is at most $\lambda$, so an absolute-value subgradient can cancel it. All coordinates and the intercept must satisfy their conditions for a full optimum.

logistic-lasso.title: Effect on odds
logistic-lasso.prompt: What odds multiplier does a one-unit increase give for a coefficient $-0.588$?
logistic-lasso.answer: The multiplier is $e^{-0.588}\approx0.555437$. This is conditional on the other fitted predictors and their measurement scale.

loss-and-risk.title: Loss versus risk
loss-and-risk.prompt: An estimator makes error $2$ in one sample. Under squared loss, what is its loss, and is that its risk?
loss-and-risk.answer: The realized loss is $4$. Risk is the expectation of such squared errors over the sampling distribution, so one error does not determine it.

loss-and-risk.title: Bias is not the whole criterion
loss-and-risk.prompt: A rule has variance $0.2$ and bias $0.4$. What is its squared-error risk?
loss-and-risk.answer: It is $0.2+0.4^2=0.36$. It beats an unbiased rule of variance $0.5$ at that parameter.

machine-repair-model.title: Failure rate in state one
machine-repair-model.prompt: With two machines and one down, why is the failure rate $\lambda$ rather than $2\lambda$?
machine-repair-model.answer: Only the one operating machine can fail. The failed machine contributes no failure clock until it is repaired.

machine-repair-model.title: Time scaling
machine-repair-model.prompt: What happens to the stationary probabilities if both $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are multiplied by $3$?
machine-repair-model.answer: They do not change because every neighbor-rate ratio is unchanged. Mean holding times are divided by three and throughput is multiplied by three.

markov-graphs.title: Rescaling a potential
markov-graphs.prompt: What happens to the distribution if one clique potential is multiplied by $4$?
markov-graphs.answer: The normalizer $Z$ is multiplied by $4$ and the distribution is unchanged. The potential is not itself the marginal distribution of the clique.

markov-graphs.title: Edge interpretation
markov-graphs.prompt: Does an edge in a Markov graph prove that its endpoints are marginally dependent?
markov-graphs.answer: No. The graph permits conditional dependence. A particular distribution can have further independences, and marginal dependence is a different statement.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-binomial-propor.title: Pooling unequal groups
maximum-likelihood-for-a-binomial-propor.prompt: Two independent groups sharing $p$ have counts $1/2$ and $8/10$. What is the pooled MLE?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-binomial-propor.answer: The pooled count is $9$ out of $12$, giving $0.75$. The unweighted average $0.65$ does not maximize the pooled likelihood.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-binomial-propor.title: Open parameter space
maximum-likelihood-for-a-binomial-propor.prompt: For zero successes in five trials with parameter space $(0,1)$, does an MLE exist?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-binomial-propor.answer: No. The likelihood approaches its supremum as $p\downarrow0$, but zero is excluded. With parameter space $[0,1]$, the MLE is zero.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-covariance-matr.title: Rank obstruction
maximum-likelihood-for-a-covariance-matr.prompt: Can the unrestricted covariance MLE be positive definite with $n=3$ and $p=4$ when the mean is unknown?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-covariance-matr.answer: No. Centering bounds the scatter rank by $n-1=2$, below four.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-covariance-matr.title: Known mean
maximum-likelihood-for-a-covariance-matr.prompt: If the mean is known rather than estimated, what scatter enters the covariance MLE?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-covariance-matr.answer: Use $n^{-1}\sum_i(x_i-\mu)(x_i-\mu)^\top$. It is centered at the known population mean, and its expectation is $\Sigma$.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-known-graph.title: Locate the graph zero
maximum-likelihood-for-a-known-graph.prompt: In a Gaussian chain with edges one–two and two–three, which matrix must have a zero in position one–three?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-known-graph.answer: The precision matrix must have that zero. The covariance between the endpoints can be nonzero.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-known-graph.title: Certify an interior fit
maximum-likelihood-for-a-known-graph.prompt: Which conditions certify a proposed positive-definite fit for a fixed Gaussian graph?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-known-graph.answer: Its precision has every prescribed non-edge zero, and its covariance matches the sample covariance on all diagonals and graph edges. Strict concavity then makes the feasible stationary point the unique maximiser.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-mean-vec.title: Covariance of an average
maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-mean-vec.prompt: For $n=8$ independent normal vectors with covariance $\operatorname{diag}(4,16)$, what is the covariance of the mean?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-mean-vec.answer: It is $\operatorname{diag}(1/2,2)$. Each covariance entry is divided by eight.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-mean-vec.title: Unequal precision
maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-mean-vec.prompt: Two scalar observations $0$ and $10$ have known variances $1$ and $4$. What common-mean MLE results?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-mean-vec.answer: Precision weights are $1$ and $1/4$, so the MLE is $(0+10/4)/(1+1/4)=2$.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-sample.title: Five centred squares
maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-sample.prompt: Five observations have centred sum of squares 20. What variance maximises the normal likelihood, and what is the unbiased estimate?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-sample.answer: The maximum-likelihood estimate divides by 5 and equals 4. The unbiased estimate divides by 4 and equals 5.

maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-sample.title: No observed variation
maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-sample.prompt: All three observations equal seven. Does the positive-variance normal family attain a maximum likelihood fit?
maximum-likelihood-for-a-normal-sample.answer: No. The likelihood grows without bound as the mean is set to seven and the positive variance tends to zero. Zero variance is outside that parameter space.

maximum-likelihood-under-the-wrong-model.title: Pseudo-true target
maximum-likelihood-under-the-wrong-model.prompt: Which part of the KL expression changes when the fitted parameter changes?
maximum-likelihood-under-the-wrong-model.answer: Only $-E_0\log f(X;\theta)$ changes. The expectation of $\log f_0$ is constant, so maximizing expected fitted log density minimizes KL when both are well-defined.

maximum-likelihood-under-the-wrong-model.title: Sandwich direction
maximum-likelihood-under-the-wrong-model.prompt: Must a misspecified Poisson model underestimate a sample mean’s variance?
maximum-likelihood-under-the-wrong-model.answer: No. The true variance is $v/n$, while the model uses $m/n$. It underestimates when $v>m$ and overestimates when $v<m$.

mean-and-variance-of-an-exponential-fami.title: Keep the sign convention
mean-and-variance-of-an-exponential-fami.prompt: An exponential family is written with numerator $y\eta+c(\eta)$ and unit dispersion. What are its mean and variance?
mean-and-variance-of-an-exponential-fami.answer: They are $-c\prime(\eta)$ and $-c\prime\prime(\eta)$. Writing $A=-c$ gives the equivalent positive-derivative convention.

mean-and-variance-of-an-exponential-fami.title: Find a zero-curvature direction
mean-and-variance-of-an-exponential-fami.prompt: What does a zero quadratic form in the covariance Hessian of a sufficient statistic mean?
mean-and-variance-of-an-exponential-fami.answer: The corresponding linear combination of sufficient statistics has variance zero and is almost surely constant. A minimal regular representation rules out such nonzero directions.

median-unbiased-estimators.title: Symmetry about the target
median-unbiased-estimators.prompt: An estimator has a continuous sampling distribution symmetric about the parameter. Is the estimator median-unbiased?
median-unbiased-estimators.answer: Yes. Continuous symmetry puts probability 1/2 on each side of the parameter, so both weak tail probabilities equal 1/2.

median-unbiased-estimators.title: Transform the target too
median-unbiased-estimators.prompt: If a positive estimator is median-unbiased for a positive parameter, is its logarithm median-unbiased for the logarithm of that parameter?
median-unbiased-estimators.answer: Yes. The logarithm is strictly increasing, so both comparisons with the transformed target correspond exactly to comparisons before transformation.

method-of-moments.title: Raw versus central moments
method-of-moments.prompt: The first two sample raw moments are three and twelve. What empirical central second moment do they imply?
method-of-moments.answer: It is $12-3^2=3$, using denominator $n$ in the empirical moments.

method-of-moments.title: An impossible binomial fit
method-of-moments.prompt: Moment matching for a binomial family with unknown count and probability produces sample mean two and central second moment three. What happens to the probability estimate?
method-of-moments.answer: The equation gives $1-3/2=-1/2$, outside the parameter space. There is no feasible exact moment solution from these two moments.

metropolis-hastings-invariance.title: Unknown target normalizer
metropolis-hastings-invariance.prompt: If π(x)=f(x)/Z, which factor cancels from the acceptance ratio, and must the proposal densities cancel too?
metropolis-hastings-invariance.answer: Z cancels. The proposal factors cancel only when q(y|x)=q(x|y).

metropolis-hastings-invariance.title: A balanced but useless transition
metropolis-hastings-invariance.prompt: Does the identity transition $P(x,\{x\})=1$ have π as an invariant distribution, and does that imply useful exploration?
metropolis-hastings-invariance.answer: Every π is invariant under the identity transition. It never moves, so invariance alone does not imply exploration or convergence from a point start.

milk-carton-example.title: A future carton
milk-carton-example.prompt: Under the same normal model, why is a prediction interval for one new carton wider than the confidence interval for the process mean?
milk-carton-example.answer: The prediction interval includes both uncertainty about the mean and fresh carton-to-carton scatter. The mean interval includes only the uncertainty about the mean.

milk-carton-example.title: An interval for which object?
milk-carton-example.prompt: Does the mean confidence interval (1.028529,1.073871) assert that 95% of cartons have volumes in that range?
milk-carton-example.answer: No. It concerns the population mean under a repeated-sampling confidence procedure. Individual-volume prediction needs a wider interval.

mine-injury-data.title: Units of the extraction coefficient
mine-injury-data.prompt: Does $e^{0.0627}$ describe a one-percent relative increase in extraction or one percentage point?
mine-injury-data.answer: One percentage point in the recorded extraction covariate. It multiplies the mean by about $1.064707$ while other recorded covariates stay fixed.

mine-injury-data.title: Absolute change at one profile
mine-injury-data.prompt: The rounded profile $(100,70,5)$ has linear predictor $0.3598$. What is the linear predictor after one more extraction percentage point, and by about how much does the fitted mean rise?
mine-injury-data.answer: The linear predictor becomes $0.4225$. The fitted mean rises from about $1.433$ to about $1.526$, an increase of about $0.0927$. That difference depends on the baseline mean.

mixture-discriminant-analysis.title: Sum before assigning the class
mixture-discriminant-analysis.prompt: Why does choosing the single most probable subclass need not give the Bayes class assignment?
mixture-discriminant-analysis.answer: A class posterior sums the contributions of all subclasses belonging to that class. Several moderate contributions can outweigh one large contribution from another class.

mixture-discriminant-analysis.title: Recover the one-subclass model
mixture-discriminant-analysis.prompt: In canonical common-covariance mixture discriminant analysis, what model results when every class has one subclass?
mixture-discriminant-analysis.answer: Linear discriminant analysis results. Quadratic discriminant analysis additionally requires allowing the covariance to differ between classes.

monotonicity-of-em.title: A partial M step
monotonicity-of-em.prompt: Must an M step find the global maximum of Q to preserve the EM ascent inequality?
monotonicity-of-em.answer: No. A generalised EM step is sufficient when it does not decrease Q relative to the current parameter, with the E-step law fixed and the required integrability and support conditions satisfied.

monotonicity-of-em.title: Values versus parameters
monotonicity-of-em.prompt: If the observed log-likelihood is nondecreasing and bounded above, what convergence follows directly?
monotonicity-of-em.answer: The likelihood values converge to a finite limit. Convergence of parameter values, stationarity and global optimality require additional arguments.

monty-hall-problem.title: Strategy versus branch
monty-hall-problem.prompt: If a standard host always chooses $B$ when able and opens $B$, must the switch probability be $2/3$?
monty-hall-problem.answer: No. Here $q=1$, so conditional on opening $B$ it is $1/2$. The unconditional always-switch strategy still wins $2/3$ of games.

monty-hall-problem.title: Ten doors
monty-hall-problem.prompt: A knowledgeable host opens eight empty unchosen doors among ten and always offers the remaining alternative. What is the switching success probability?
monty-hall-problem.answer: It is $9/10$, because the initial choice was wrong with that probability.

multi-server-and-finite-capacity-queues.title: Capacity convention
multi-server-and-finite-capacity-queues.prompt: In M/M/2/5, how many customers can wait when the system is full?
multi-server-and-finite-capacity-queues.answer: Three wait and two are in service, because the capacity five counts everyone in the system.

multi-server-and-finite-capacity-queues.title: Finite overload
multi-server-and-finite-capacity-queues.prompt: Does $\lambda>c\mu$ prevent a stationary law for M/M/$c$/$K$?
multi-server-and-finite-capacity-queues.answer: No. A positive-rate finite irreducible chain has a stationary law. High offered load instead produces blocking.

multinomial-central-limit-theorem.title: The missing degree of freedom
multinomial-central-limit-theorem.prompt: For four categories with all probabilities positive, what is the rank of diag(p)−ppᵀ?
multinomial-central-limit-theorem.answer: Its rank is three. The sum-to-one constraint removes the all-ones direction.

multinomial-central-limit-theorem.title: Combining cells
multinomial-central-limit-theorem.prompt: With p=(0.2,0.3,0.5), what is Cov(p̂₁,p̂₂) for n=100?
multinomial-central-limit-theorem.answer: It is −p₁p₂/n=−0.0006. The category counts share a fixed total.

multinomial-logistic-regression.title: A common score shift
multinomial-logistic-regression.prompt: What happens to softmax probabilities if the same constant is added to every class score?
multinomial-logistic-regression.answer: They are unchanged: the common exponential factor cancels between each numerator and the denominator.

multinomial-logistic-regression.title: Odds and a probability factor
multinomial-logistic-regression.prompt: Two class scores are 0 and 0. Only the second score is raised by log 3. By what factors do the odds of the second class against the first, and the second class probability, change?
multinomial-logistic-regression.answer: The odds change from 1 to 3, a factor of 3. The probability changes from 1/2 to 3/4, a factor of 3/2.

multiple-comparisons.title: Counting pairs
multiple-comparisons.prompt: How many pairwise differences arise from six group means?

multiple-comparisons.title: Independence requirement
multiple-comparisons.answer: No. It follows from the union bound, which holds under arbitrary dependence when the individual error bounds are valid.

multiple-linear-regression.title: An extra dependent column
multiple-linear-regression.prompt: A design has two binary columns, and a third column equals their sum. Is the least-squares coefficient vector still unique?
multiple-linear-regression.answer: No. The new column is an exact linear combination of two others. The fitted response projection can be unique while the coefficient representation is not.

multiple-linear-regression.title: Why the residuals sum to zero
multiple-linear-regression.prompt: Why does a design that contains a column of ones force the least-squares residuals to sum to zero?
multiple-linear-regression.answer: The normal equations make that column orthogonal to the residual. The column of ones sums the residuals, so the sum is zero.

non-negative-matrix-factorisation.title: Scale nonuniqueness
non-negative-matrix-factorisation.prompt: If WH reconstructs a matrix, what happens after multiplying the first column of W by three and dividing the matching first row of H by three?
non-negative-matrix-factorisation.answer: The product is unchanged because each affected outer-product term has one factor multiplied and the other divided by three.

non-negative-matrix-factorisation.title: Rank-one impossibility
non-negative-matrix-factorisation.prompt: Why can the worked-example matrix [[1,2],[3,4]] not be reproduced exactly with r=1?
non-negative-matrix-factorisation.answer: Its determinant is 1·4−2·3=−2, so it has rank two. A product of an m×1 and a 1×n matrix has rank at most one.

normal-inverse-gamma-prior.title: Which variance conditions on the centre?
normal-inverse-gamma-prior.prompt: The joint posterior has parameters $\alpha_n,\beta_n,\kappa_n,\mu_n$. What is the inverse-Gamma shape after conditioning additionally on a fixed $\mu$?
normal-inverse-gamma-prior.answer: It is $\alpha_n+1/2$. The scale is $\beta_n+\kappa_n(\mu-\mu_n)^2/2$; this differs from marginalising over $\mu$.

normal-inverse-gamma-prior.title: Scale and variance
normal-inverse-gamma-prior.prompt: A Student marginal for a normal centre has more than two degrees of freedom and squared scale s². Is its variance equal to s²?
normal-inverse-gamma-prior.answer: No. The variance is the squared scale times ν/(ν−2), which is larger than s².

normal-normal-model.title: Same sum, same known-variance update
normal-normal-model.prompt: Under a fixed known variance, do samples (4,6,8) and (5,6,7) produce the same posterior for μ with the same prior?
normal-normal-model.answer: Yes. They have the same size and sample mean. Their likelihoods differ only by a factor constant in μ.

normal-normal-model.title: Two positive precisions
normal-normal-model.prompt: With a positive prior variance and a positive sampling variance for the mean, why is the posterior variance of μ smaller than both of those variances?
normal-normal-model.answer: The posterior precision is the sum of two positive precisions. The reciprocal of a sum of positive terms is smaller than either reciprocal, so the posterior variance is smaller than both the prior variance and the sampling variance of the mean.

nuisance-parameters.title: Changing the target
nuisance-parameters.prompt: Is the variance always a nuisance parameter in a normal model?
nuisance-parameters.answer: No. It is a nuisance for a mean-only question, but becomes the target when variability is the scientific quantity of interest.

nuisance-parameters.title: Information calculation
nuisance-parameters.prompt: For $I=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}4&2\\2&4\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, compare the target variance bounds with and without estimating the second parameter.
nuisance-parameters.answer: The inverse first diagonal entry is $1/(4-4/4)=1/3$. With the second parameter known, the bound is $1/4$.

null-distribution-of-hotelling-s.title: The univariate check
null-distribution-of-hotelling-s.prompt: When p=1, what does the scaled Hotelling statistic become?
null-distribution-of-hotelling-s.answer: The scale factor is one and T²=t², with law F₁,ₙ₋₁ under the normal mean null.

null-distribution-of-hotelling-s.title: A singular sample covariance
null-distribution-of-hotelling-s.prompt: Can the stated inverse-covariance statistic be used when p≥n?
null-distribution-of-hotelling-s.answer: No. The centered scatter rank is at most n−1<p, so the sample covariance has no ordinary inverse.

observational-study.title: What the label fixes
observational-study.prompt: Investigators record which treatment each patient received but do not assign it. Does describing the study as observational determine which regression should be fitted?
observational-study.answer: No. Observational describes the origin of the exposure. A regression, if one is used, is a separate choice of summary.

observational-study.title: Two different randomisations
observational-study.prompt: Why can a study draw a random sample and still be observational?
observational-study.answer: Random sampling chooses who is observed. Random assignment chooses a treatment. A random sample can receive treatments chosen by clinicians.

one-hidden-layer-approximates-continuous.title: Unrestricted output
one-hidden-layer-approximates-continuous.prompt: Why can a network with sigmoid hidden units represent the constant function 3?
one-hidden-layer-approximates-continuous.answer: A hidden unit with zero input weights and zero bias has value 1/2. Giving it output weight 6 produces the constant 3.

one-hidden-layer-approximates-continuous.title: A discontinuous target
one-hidden-layer-approximates-continuous.prompt: Can continuous sigmoid networks converge uniformly to a step with a jump on [0,1]?
one-hidden-layer-approximates-continuous.answer: No. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, whereas the target has a jump.

one-sample-t-pivot.title: Residual directions
one-sample-t-pivot.prompt: A normal sample of size 25 is studentised at the true mean. How many degrees of freedom does the pivot have?
one-sample-t-pivot.answer: It has 24. Estimating the mean removes one of the 25 orthogonal directions, and the sample variance uses the rest.

one-sample-t-pivot.title: Centre the numerator
one-sample-t-pivot.prompt: If a normal population mean is μ=2 but a statistic is centred at μ0=0, is its law the central t law?
one-sample-t-pivot.answer: No. Its noncentrality is √n(2−0)/σ; the central t law applies when the numerator is centred at the true mean.

one-sample-t-test.title: Two tails under symmetry
one-sample-t-test.prompt: A positive t statistic is compared with a symmetric Student null distribution. Why is the two-sided p-value twice the upper-tail probability?
one-sample-t-test.answer: The null distribution is symmetric about zero, so the lower tail beyond the negative statistic has the same probability as the upper tail.

one-sample-t-test.title: Moving the null
one-sample-t-test.prompt: The null mean moves halfway from its old value toward the sample mean, and the estimated standard error stays fixed. What happens to the absolute t statistic?
one-sample-t-test.answer: It is halved. The statistic is the departure of the sample mean from the null, divided by that standard error.

paired-samples.title: Differences, not raw rows
paired-samples.prompt: Eight independent pairs are analysed by a paired t statistic. How many degrees of freedom does the reference law have?
paired-samples.answer: Seven. The eight differences are the observations, and their mean is estimated.

paired-samples.title: Equal sizes are not pairs
paired-samples.prompt: Two separate samples each contain eight observations. Why is that not enough to justify a paired analysis?
paired-samples.answer: Pairing needs a match supplied by the design, such as two measurements on one specimen. Equal sample sizes do not create those matches.

pearson-chi-squared-approximation.title: The missing direction
pearson-chi-squared-approximation.prompt: Why do four specified cell probabilities give three degrees of freedom?
pearson-chi-squared-approximation.answer: The four counts must sum to the fixed total. Only three count deviations can vary freely.

pearson-chi-squared-approximation.title: A zero observation
pearson-chi-squared-approximation.prompt: A cell has expected count 8 and observed count zero. What does it contribute?
pearson-chi-squared-approximation.answer: Its contribution is (0−8)²/8=8; an observed zero does not make the denominator zero.

pearson-dispersion-ratio.title: A different variance function
pearson-dispersion-ratio.prompt: The counts 1, 2, 8 and 9 have squared deviations 16, 9, 9 and 16 about the mean 5. What Pearson sum and dispersion ratio does the variance function μ² produce on three residual degrees of freedom?
pearson-dispersion-ratio.answer: The sum is 50/25 = 2. On three residual degrees of freedom the ratio is 2/3 = 0.666667.

pearson-dispersion-ratio.title: What gets scaled?
pearson-dispersion-ratio.prompt: If a common dispersion estimate is 4 and fitted means are held fixed, by what factors do coefficient variances and standard errors change?
pearson-dispersion-ratio.answer: Variances multiply by 4 and standard errors by √4 = 2. A dispersion correction changes uncertainty rather than directly multiplying fitted means.

pearson-test-with-estimated-parameters.title: Identifiable directions
pearson-test-with-estimated-parameters.prompt: Six fixed cells are fitted with a regular identifiable two-parameter grouped model. What is the reference degrees of freedom?

pearson-test-with-estimated-parameters.title: What the fit cannot adjust
